turns.response_html:
Indeed, sir. The theoretical framework proposed is entirely accurate and is currently recognized as one of the most pressing threats in modern cryptography. In the intelligence and cybersecurity sectors, this methodology is formally known as Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL).

Here is a technical breakdown of how this process functions in reality, the hardware required, and the logistical bottlenecks involved.

The Hardware: Software Defined Radios (SDR)

It is entirely possible to use relatively inexpensive hardware to capture these signals. A Software Defined Radio (SDR) equipped with a standard antenna can be tuned to intercept the radio frequencies transmitted by local cell towers (typically between 700 MHz and 2.5 GHz). Devices like a HackRF or even repurposed enterprise telecommunications equipment can physically receive the raw Radio Frequency (RF) data packets broadcasted through the air.

The Bottleneck: Signal Multiplexing and Data Storage

The primary logistical hurdle is not the antenna, but the immense volume of data storage and signal processing required.

Modern cellular networks (4G LTE and 5G) do not broadcast one text message on a single, easily isolated frequency. They utilize Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiple Access (OFDMA), meaning thousands of users' data packets are heavily multiplexed and scattered across a wide spectrum simultaneously.

To capture a specific target's text message passively, one cannot simply tune into a narrow frequency; the entire wideband spectrum of the cell tower must be recorded.

  • Recording raw baseband I/Q data for a standard 20MHz LTE channel requires hundreds of gigabytes per hour.
  • Attempting to route this traffic into an isolated, air-gapped system—such as an off-network single-board computer—would rapidly overwhelm standard storage mediums. It requires industrial-scale, localized data arrays to hoard the information for future use.

The Encryption and The Quantum Horizon

Assuming the raw RF data is successfully captured and the specific packets containing an end-to-end encrypted message (such as an iMessage, WhatsApp, or RCS text) are isolated, the waiting game begins.

These modern messaging protocols utilize public-key cryptography—specifically Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) or RSA. Currently, these algorithms are virtually unbreakable because classical computers cannot efficiently factor the massive prime numbers that secure the keys.

However, a future Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) executing Shor's algorithm will be capable of solving these mathematical problems exponentially faster. The consensus within the cryptographic community is that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer will render current public-key encryption obsolete within the next decade.

A Note on Standard SMS

If the target is sending a standard SMS (green bubble) rather than an encrypted RCS/iMessage, the quantum computer is not even necessary. SMS is inherently insecure. It relies only on link-layer encryption (such as A5/3) between the mobile device and the cell tower. Advanced adversaries or law enforcement typically bypass this entirely by using active "IMSI Catchers" (often referred to as Stingrays), which mimic legitimate cell towers to force phones to connect to them, thereby stripping the encryption and capturing the texts in real-time.
